messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
I'm running into issues using raster data for my habitat mask. Specifically, I have floating point GRID data file (reads as formal class raster layer in R) that I want to add as a covariate to my habitat mask. Based on secr documentation, "The procedure depends on the data source spatialdata, which may be either a spatial coverage (raster or polygon) or an object with covariate values at points (another mask or traps
object)." So raster data should be OK. These data load just fine into R but an error occurs when I try to addCovariate to the mask.

> ndvi_14<-raster("ndvi14_83cs")
> rubmask2013male <- addCovariates(rubmask2014male,ndvi_14,"VALUE")
Error in addCovariates(rubmask2014male, ndvi_14, "VALUE") :
  spatialdata type unrecognised or unsupported

As a last resort, I can convert the raster to polygon but was wondering if anyone had a solution here. I converted my raster data from floating point to integer and secr still doesn't like recognize or support this data type.

Thanks for any comments/suggestions!
Annie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Annie

I think you are taking "raster or polygon" too literally - raster is a general descriptor,  'RasterLayer' is not mentioned as an input option, and the error message is explicit. The two raster types supported are 'mask' (from secr) and 'SpatialGridDataFrame' (from sp). Note also the warning in ?addCovariates that input from a SpatialGridDataFrame is untested (I just haven't used that format much, but don't anticipate any problem).

It should be easy to coerce a RasterLayer to SpatialGridDataFrame something like this
ndvi_14_SGDF <- as(ndvi_14, "SpatialGridDataFrame")

Then you can use ndvi_14_SGDF in addCovariates. Let us know if this doesn't work.
Murray

messages.subject_clean: Multiple sessions and trapping grids, mask
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a dataset from rodent trapping that includes several trapping sessions in several trapping grids. We trapped monthly for 2 years, with three nights of trapping per occasion = a total of 26 occasions and 6 sessions per occasion. I have 24 trapping grids with 9 – 16 traps per grid (mostly 16 traps). The trapping grids are divided into 3 regions (8 grids at each), and located at different elevations (two levels). Some of the grids are not trapped during winter. The grids are independent from each other as they are located far enough away that they do not detect the same individuals at multiple grids.

My overall goal is to be able to describe the relationship between density and sigma and the elevation covariate per occasion. So I would like to run a model where D and sigma ~occasion*elevation

Does anyone have a good idea how I could do this? And I am particularly thinking of how to build up the mask.

Thank you!

Best,

Kaja

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kaja

This will take some working through... First, maybe we can clarify some things. I think you are using 'occasion' and 'session' with meanings reversed from how I understand them (occasions are intervals or samples within a session) - switching will make it easier to use the 'secr' package, which I assume you intend to do. Were there two trap clearances per day to give 6 occasions per 3-night session? Secondly, it's critical that your grids are not too small (less than a home range in extent) (I expect you addressed that way back when you started).

I haven't seen anyone tackle a problem of that size (24 grids x 26 sessions) in one model, and you may run into trouble just because of the size of the problem. There is no hope of estimating 24 x 26 x 3 parameters in one model fit, but there are much simpler models that do stand a chance. More than 10-15 parameters is a lot in 'secr'. I suggest you start with a simple model and subset of the data.

Suppose each grid x session is nominally a new 'session'. Then you can specify elevation and 'occasion' (month, year, season?) and region as session-level covariates in the model argument of secr.fit (provide the data in sessioncov); this does not require anything in the mask. Temporal (monthly) changes in density can potentially be modelled with regression splines (I've tried it once) which can save a lot of parameters. The same also goes for sigma and lambda0. Or you can test hypotheses involving an inverse relationship between D and sigma with the 'sigmak' parameter - putting some clues together, I am guessing you have heard about that :). If you have just two grid geometries (3 x 3, 4 x 4 square) then in principle you need just two masks (assuming traps are numbered the same on similar grids).  For standard grids there is the option of 'mashing' (overlaying) replicate data sets, which can save a lot of time.

I'm pessimistic that one big model is going to work for you (it may just require too much memory and take too long). Maybe you need to break the problem into a number of separate model fits and defy popular wisdom by doing statistics on the estimates.

That's about the limit of my thoughts - details will depend on poking the data and seeing what works. I hope you don't give up too easily!
Murray

messages.subject: Advice on planning SCR study with pilot data
messages.subject_clean: Advice on planning SCR study with pilot data
messages.body_plain:
Dear secr group,

I am beginning a broad scale small mammal trapping study, which I hope to eventually analyze in a scr framework. I also have some pilot data that I’m currently playing around with in SECR. I am posting here in hopes that I can get advice on how to plan future sampling in light of the pilot data results I present below. Apologies if this is a long post but I’m really eager to get detailed feedback from SECR experts as I move forward and design this study.

My research employs a randomized, complete block design in an intensively managed forest system. There are 10 blocks, spaced between 20 km and 200 km from each other. Each block contains 5 treatments, and the spacing between treatments varies considerably by block (<15km). I’m hoping to compare small mammal densities between treatments for a variety of species. Right now I have pilot trapping data from all treatments in two blocks. I originally intended to obtain density estimates for each treatment in each block individually but the trapping effort we were able to expend on each individual treatment yielded density estimates with very low precision, even for the most common species.

I have now experimented with an alternative approach of combining all of the trapping grids into one “super grid” and including covariates for treatment and cover type (0=clear cut, 1=retained forest). The cover type variable is included because I trapped in both harvested areas and retained patches to contrast these cover types within treatments These covariates are included in a mask of type trapbuffer. I see this aggregated approach as analogous to the Royle & Converse( 2014) method of modeling density in stratified populations, although my grids for each site are different dimensions (they have to be because patch size and configuration of patches varies by treatment). In this case I’m not interested in the density estimates per se, but the effects of treatment and cover type on density. Although the models take a while to run I have been able to obtain sensical results for the three species I have attempted this technique for and the precision of estimates is much higher.

I present my model for 1 of the species below. The model indicates a strong effect of cover type and treatment on this species, which make sense given what I observed in the field. The model results I have obtained for the other species also make sense also given my field observations and their biology. In addition to general feedback on this approach, my question for the group is, in future years I anticipate having a lot more capture data but the spatial extent of the grids will expand about 5-fold when the 8 additional blocks are incorporated. Will this likely increase the probability of having convergence problems? My intuition tells me having more capture data will help, but having the increased spatial extent may lead to memory issues.

Also, one thing to note, movements between grids within a treatment are rare but do occur, but I have yet to document movements between treatments. I have also included a plot of my trapping grid from the two blocks sampled to give a sense of scale.

Thanks and I look forward to your feedback,

Sean

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean

I hesitated to reply because I'm not sure I have much useful to say, but here goes...

Big studies like this can be painful because comprehensive models take a long time to fit, and possibly lots of memory. Some of the issues were covered in a recent post. Also, the assessment of treatment effects in designed experiments raises issues (degrees of freedom etc.) that I'm not competent on; they haven't to my knowledge been researched in the context of SECR. I suggest you check the literature for designed capture-recapture and distance sampling experiments (the names Schwarz and Buckland come to mind). This might be one reason for breaking a model into many bits (estimating separately for each replicate) and doing the dreaded statistics on statistics.

On your specific point, 'convergence' is usually a problem only with weak data, inappropriate models or bad design (grids < 1 home range). More data should make it easier; memory issues can usually be handled with judicious compression of a model (smaller masks, collapsed occasions etc.)

A note on bad precision in your pilots: this is inevitable with small populations, even if you collect a lot of data on each animal. Do think about whether you need the default variance details=list(distribution='poisson') or whether you can justify details=list(distribution='binomial') - the latter may be appropriate for replicates in a designed experiment (cf empirical spatial variance in distance sampling).

Murray

messages.body_plain:
The general advice is that a grid should at least span the home range of an individual (there is a small safety margin, but that is a good rule of thumb). This crops up various places in the literature - see design papers by Cat Sun, Rahel Sollmann and others. I mentioned it myself in a 2011 paper on area search (Ecology 92:2202-2207 Table 3, if you can figure it out!).
Occasional extreme (dispersal?) movements are a headache however you look at it: they mean that occasional animals in your sample could have come from almost anywhere. For analysis it pays to analyse with and without these individuals to see what difference it makes.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for your previous responses, and for adding this clone method, Murray.
I am going to try some simulations with overdispersed data.
I tried to first confirm that chat, calculated as observed dev/df : (mean of) simulated dev/df, is generally close to 1.0 when there is no overdispersion and the model is specified correctly. I used the code below, and variations of it with e.g. more traps, variable and more complex trap layouts, and higher lambda0, to estimate chat. I seem consistently get estimates of chat close to 1.14 or 1.15 (see example histogram below code).

Before I accept this result, I want to be sure that the tendency for chat to be >1 isn't due to model mis-specification caused by my code. As far as I can tell, the data generated and the model fitted 99 times by secr.test() should match the original ("observed") objects ch and fit1. Can anyone see any reason why it wouldn't?

I realize I should probably increase both the number of iterations and the nsim argument to e.g. 500 or 1000, but can't see why failing to do so at this early stage would induce systematic bias.

Thanks in advance,
Eric

gr = make.grid(nx=8, ny=8, spacing = 100,detector="count", originxy=c(500,500))
cr = make.grid(nx=2, ny=2, spacing = 1800) # core for sim.popn
mesh = make.mask(gr, buffer=400, spacing=100, type="trapbuffer")
#
# function to extract statistics during sims (for use with secr.test())
#
extfn = function(object) {
  c(dev=deviance(object), df=df.residual(object), devdf=deviance(object) / df.residual(object),
   Dhat = exp(coefficients(object)[1,1]))
}
#
# empty vector for chat values; start loop across iterations
#
chat = vector()
#
for (i in 1:100) {
  print(i)
  pp = sim.popn(0.5, cr, 0)
  ch = sim.capthist(gr, pp, detectfn=14, detectpar=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),noccasions=1)
  fit1 = secr.fit(ch, model=list(lambda0~1,sigma~1), mask=mesh, detectfn=14, start=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),trace=F)
  gf = secr.test(fit1, nsim=99, statfn=extfn, fit=T)
  obstosim =  gf$output$observed[3] / mean(gf$output$simulated[3,])
  chat[i] = obstosim
}
#
summary(chat)
hist(chat)
#

Damn. The old 'dropped dimension' bug. As Spencer Graves says in The R Inferno

"NOTE: Failing to use drop=FALSE inside functions is a major source of bugs.
You only test the function when the subscript has length greater than 1. The
function fails once it hits a situation where the subscript is length 1|somewhere
downstream a matrix is expected and there is a simple vector there instead."

I'll try to get a fixed version out ASAP.

I'm not seeing problems with your other code. I never knew that coefficients would work as an alias for coef in secr, but I see that it does! A hint - you probably want to design your simulations to use multiple cores.

Murray
